entry.title: Crack-a-nut (no sponsor, I wish though)
entry.content:
This is a big one. As noted in a previous post, some Northern nutcrackers have been pouring into Belgium. The hype was so big it even made the national news. Specifically, it is the macrorhynchos/slender-billed/Siberian subspecies (multiple denominations, though slender-billed seems a funny choice given its scientific name). Normally found between the Ural mountains and north-east China, the slender-billed nutcracker can erupt out of its range when pine cone shortages occur, causing it to search for food as far as western Europe. There were some 300 nutcrackers recorded in 1968 in Great Britain, but the original source for this in the Wikipedia article on the northern nutcracker is no longer available. After dredging Google’s muddied search results (there was also a movie release of “The Nutcracker” in the same year), this archive article puts the 1968 GB count of Northern nutcrackers at 315, with no specification of the subspecies. This paper (what am I, a scientist still?) recorded 4000 observations in The Netherlands between June 1968–June 1969 but gives no estimate on the total amount of birds, only noting that 100 of them were ringed. I did not find a source citing the number of individuals. In any case, the number of observations today has not paralleled that of 1968, but with almost 1200 observations this year to date we are well underway to have similar numbers to 1968. It’s also worth noting that almost all (99.2%) of macrorhynchos observations on waarnemingen in The Netherlands since 1971 occurred this year! So it’s special, very special.

Northern nutcrackers occur in Europe every year, and the (less rare yet still rare) thick-billed (nucifraga caryocatactes caryocatactes) subspecies, its normal range being Europe, is not seen more often this year than other years. The fact that the invasion is specifically by the slender-billed subspecies (macrorhynchos), with birds travelling all the way from Siberia, is worth some more emphasis than VRT gives it.

So naturally, I jump on a train taking me to Leuven, where I rent an electric bluebike on which I have horrible posture because the frames are too small for a normal human being of 1m83. Other than that and the resulting back pains, great service (no sponsor). I stop at ‘t Smullerke (no sponsor) for a broodje gerookte zalmsalade and make my way to Heverleebos (no sponsor), facing the 10,000 students on the Tiensebaan, none of whom could name a single traffic rule.

It’s still a quiet moment in the year for birding and even though the sun is out, most birds are hard to spot because not all the leaves have fallen yet. First contact is with a majestic blue tit holding on to its nut for dear life.

Blue tit on a beach nut in Heverleebos on 4 November 2026. Majestic.
Same tit, same nut.
×
Blue tit on a beach nut in Heverleebos on 4 November 2026. Majestic.
×
Same tit, same nut.

Next I snag a slightly better picture than previously of a crested tit and a not-so-great-as-before picture of a nuthatch. You win some, you lose some.

Crested tit, now with extra pointy head feathers.
No tits here, just a red breast(ed nuthatch).
×
Crested tit, now with extra pointy head feathers.
×
No tits here, just a red breast(ed nuthatch).

I walk around for a few hours before I decide to just go to the last known location of the nutcracker reported on waarnemingen.be. The first friendly birder I find there doesn’t even need bribing with my nicnacskes to tell me that the bird was just there, but I give him some anyway. We stand around for a couple of minutes – him, a man that has seen The Bird, and me, who’s rarest bird found to date is a zitting cisticola – talking about how he tried to spot the nutcracker three days in a row last week with no luck. He then leaves for the office (a birder on a Wednesday noon with a job hanging around Heverleebos? Must be nice). I decide to wait it out at the last known location, all the while keeping an eye on a group of about 6 people in the distance. As another man-with-camera walks by towards the group, I tell him to give me a sign should they see something. Even before he arrives, the group that til just now looked inert, jumps into a frenzy, pointing all sorts of lenses at a tree.

The Moment and I both arrive, commemorated by the following pictures.

Slender-billed nutcracker in Heverleebos on 4 November 2026.
Brother hast thou nuts? For this tree is empty and I am but skin and bones.
Maybe some nuts have fallen to the ground? They do be doing that. Let me check.
It's much warmer here than in Siberia.
×
Slender-billed nutcracker in Heverleebos on 4 November 2026.
×
Brother hast thou nuts? For this tree is empty and I am but skin and bones.
×
Maybe some nuts have fallen to the ground? They do be doing that. Let me check.
×
It's much warmer here than in Siberia.

It stays for a couple of minutes in the same tree on a branch about 3 meters from the ground, then moves to a couple of low branches in the forest, before sitting on a branch and on the ground a couple of meters from where I’m standing along with some ten other people. Lucky my camera has stabilisation, cause I’m shaking from the encounter. As noted by VRT, the bird is not shy at all: it is not used to seeing people, so it also does not perceive us as a threat (although who would be afraid of a guy handing out nicnacskes to strangers?).

Anything else I still experience that day has become irrelevant, even the frame size of the bluebike on the way home.

entry.title: Crane hunt part 2
entry.content:
There’s a feeling I get, when I look to the West, except when crane migration is underway, which is when I am usually more fond of the East. For now, no significant eastern wind has blown any cranes off-track, so I was particularly excited to head eastward to Köln. Unfortunately, I learned that Köln lies beyond the typical western migration route. Indeed, barely any cranes are reported over Cologne, although I am wary of the data, which comes from a user base heavily concentrated in Belgium and The Netherlands (see below, Source: observation.org and OpenTopoMap).

Heatmap of common crane observations between 1 October and 5 November.
×
Heatmap of common crane observations between 1 October and 5 November.

Anyway, Crane hunt part 2 yields no sightings, however, Cologne was still a success, with 4 new lifers! First, in central Cologne, two parakeet species live: the Alexandrine parakeet and the rose-ringed parakeet, the former of which is a new lifer to me. Their colourful presence feels off, and the pictures feel like they are taken in a zoo, because both parakeets are feral: descendants from escaped or released domesticated parakeets. Looking at it, it’s obvious that it belongs in its native colourful South Asian habitat and not in the drab streets of Cologne.

Alexandrine parakeet in Cologne on 31 October 2026.
×
Alexandrine parakeet in Cologne on 31 October 2026.

On Sunday, we took a hike in the Wahner Heide forest, which finally yielded the long-awaited sighting of the extremely cute Eurasian treecreeper. Very similar to the more common short-toed treecreeper, it has a lighter belly, shorter bill and a different call. Pics aren’t the best as light conditions weren’t optimal, but together with the clear sound bits I am confident this is a certhia familiaris. Both occur in these parts, whereas this one does not occur in the western part of Belgium where I live. Going east was therefore not futile bird-wise.

Backside of a European treecreeper on 1 November 2026 in Wahner Heide, Köln (DE).
×
Backside of a European treecreeper on 1 November 2026 in Wahner Heide, Köln (DE).

Along the path there’s many great spotted woodpeckers foraging, goldcrests, nuthatches and robins. About ten minutes after the treecreeper success, Merlin indicates the possible presence of a crested tit, the punkest of tits. We are able to find it but the best picture I manage to snag is not great, so I’ve also included the depiction of the Haubenmeise from the information panel on birds of the forest. I have since taken a (slightly) better picture of a crested tit, which I’ll post shortly.

A fierce goldcrest.
Another goldcrest showing off.
Great spotted woodpecker (male) on a mossy tree.
Crested tit (I promise).
Fake crested tit.
×
A fierce goldcrest.
×
Another goldcrest showing off.
×
Great spotted woodpecker (male) on a mossy tree.
×
Crested tit (I promise).
×
Fake crested tit.

I’ll gladly take this (and any) opportunity to share the following wonderful meme a user named AsherWare posted in 2016 on imgur (its original source is unknown, this is the earliest known appearance of its usage):


The colossal tit (parus colossus, definitely not Linnaeus, somewhere 2016-ish) is one of the most destructive of the tit species on the British Isles, known for its crushing of hopes and dreams through its frequent media appearances and conservative policies. Its largest single-event impact thus far is the shrinkage of the UK’s GDP by at least 6%.¹

¹ Bloom et al., The Economic Impact of Brexit

entry.title: East Canada unknowns
entry.content:
Since the August east Canada trip of 2026, there have been lurking in my mind a couple of unidentified birds. For some, I have an idea but no ID. In such cases, the bird enthusiasts over at r/whatsthisbird are always keen to help. I asked for IDs of the following east Canadian birds ranging from Toronto to Tadoussac.

UB1: August 1, Toronto Islands, ON
UB2: August 5, Madawaska, Algonquin Provincial Park, ON
UB3: August 6, Booth's Rock Trail, Algonquin Provincial Park, ON
UB4: August 8, Parc National de la Mauricie, QC
UB5: August 9, St Paulin, QC
UB6: August 12, Tadoussac, QC
UB7: August 14, La Malbaie, QC
×
UB1: August 1, Toronto Islands, ON
×
UB2: August 5, Madawaska, Algonquin Provincial Park, ON
×
UB3: August 6, Booth's Rock Trail, Algonquin Provincial Park, ON
×
UB4: August 8, Parc National de la Mauricie, QC
×
UB5: August 9, St Paulin, QC
×
UB6: August 12, Tadoussac, QC
×
UB7: August 14, La Malbaie, QC

Strong consensus on r/whatsthisbird that my hunch of a female brown-headed cowbird for UB1 (unknown bird #1) was correct: the streaking on the body does not contrast enough for a female red-winged blackbird. UB2 is a sparrow, but it could be Lincoln’s sparrow or a swamp or song sparrow. Strong narrow streaking on the belly points to Lincoln’s sparrow, but there’s no reports of those in early August. A swamp sparrow is more likely. UB2 will remain unsolved without hearing the bird sing.

Likewise, UB3 remains a mystery. Flycatchers are a nightmare to distinguish if you don’t hear them sing, especially if you only have a picture of their belly side. Even Peter, former Algonquin park guide that we met on the trail who was also looking at this very same bird, couldn’t tell which bird it was. Maybe a future post should detail our lovely encounter with Peter.

UB4 has two plausible options: a breeding female Blackpoll warbler or immature female pine warbler could work, but the overall lack of colour in the picture leads me to have reservations about definitively saying this is X or Y.

Thrushes give me ID headaches, so for UB5 we are lucky that reddit thinks this is a Swainson’s thrush (dwerglijster). There’s a faint pale eye ring, the spotting on the body seems to match, and I remember that my overall impression of this bird was that it was smaller than a blackbird. With some confidence we can therefore ID UB5 as Swainson’s thrush.

UB6 can be a ‘generic’ black-headed gull (kokmeeuw), a Franklin’s gull or Bonaparte’s gull (kleine kokmeeuw). The picture does not allow to see whether there is a thick white eye ring or what the colour of the legs is (this picture was taken with my phone as we were on the whale watching boat at the time and I didn’t dare take my camera out for risk of whale splashing), so we turn to the ranges of these gulls on allaboutbirds.org. On August 12 there’s only one of those three which occurs very regularly in Tadoussac. Additionally, I feel like my camera should be able to record the much wider white eye ring on Franklin’s. UB6 is therefore a Bonaparte’s gull, as also suggested by reddit.

Least flycatcher seems to work best for UB7, given the relatively bold pale eye ring (other flycatchers such as Adler’s have thinner eye rings), the two pale wing bars and the light-coloured underside (others are more olive/buff). So least flycatcher for UB7 it is!

All in all, pulling 4 new bird species out of these pictures without accompanying sound bits is more than I had dared to hope for, bringing the species total to 151.

entry.title: Crane hunt part 1
entry.content:
Common crane (grus grus) migration through Europe is underway from Scandinavia and northern Germany to the south. There’s scattered reports all over the eastern parts of Belgium, exploding in the last couple of days. Chances are slim that a lot of the action happens over Ghent, which would require eastern winds blowing birds west. With dominant west and south-west wind this week, it’s highly unlikely that any cranes will be spotted over Bourgoyen. But I made fresh coffee and I have a warm jacket, so out we go.

No cranes yet. Luckily, there’s always the cute long-tailed tit to fall back on. A lot of barnacle geese flying over and resting at Afgraving. If the map on Wikipedia is to be trusted, these are mostly the Siberian population of barnacle geese, which winters in The Netherlands, Germany and Belgium. Fun wiki-fact: the Dutch common name and scientific name (brandgans and branta leucopsis) apparently derive from Old Norse Brandgás, meaning ‘burnt goose’.

One long-tailed tit near Afgraving on 20 October 2026.

Barnacle geese flying south over Afgraving on 20 October 2026.

I’m free on Saturday, so I’m thinking of a plan to perhaps try to head east to catch some migrating cranes. I’m also dying to find a nutcracker, multiple of which have poured down south into Belgium, one seemingly residing for a couple of days now in Heverleebos. Hard to spot cranes in a dense forest, though.

entry.title: Early birding
entry.content:
The early bird has to drive to Antwerp on a Sunday morning, but the even earlier birder manages to get some birding done even before that. No groundbreaking observations but a very photogenic wren and a kestrel being harassed by two crows. The shot of the kestrel illustrates that other inconvenient truth a friendly birder holding a 600 mm lens told me recently: you can never have enough millimeters.

Eurasian wren posing on a Sunday morning in Bourgoyen on 18 October 2026.

Common kestrel landing in a field near Valkenhuis.

Monday mornings are extremely quiet once you get out in the fields compared to Sundays. Without human distractions, I manage to spot a female hen harrier flying north over the Oude Kale valley. Unlike what the Dutch name would have you believe (blauwe kiekendief), the female harrier is brown and not blue, with a distinctive white rump.

Female hen harrier flying over Merendree on 20 October 2026.

Along the track I hear (multiple?) lesser spotted woodpeckers calling. I can’t find them, so the picture provided with the audio bite is by Yves Hoebeke from waarnemingen.be. Unlike the far more common greater spotted woodpecker, the lesser does not have a red lower belly.

Kleine bonte specht by Yves Hoebeke in Harelbeke on 22 September 2026. Licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

entry.title: Evening with barn owl pellets
entry.content:
Yesterday, as one does on a typical Friday evening, the season of pellet dissecting with the Kerkuilwerkgroep and Natuurpunt has begun with a barn owl from 2025 out of the Bourgoyen. Many more pellets than we can handle, but I manage to finish five, with the short-tailed field vole (aardmuis) spanning the crown of 4 finds (example in first picture). There’s also white-toothed shrew (huisspitsmuis), two common pine voles (ondergrondse woelmuis), common shrew (gewone bosspitsmuis) and a long-tailed field mouse (gewone bosmuis).

Short-tailed field vole out of barn owl pellet from Bourgoyen.

All determinations are checked by Johan, Norbert or Rik of the Kerkuilwerkgroep and the data is logged and used to keep track of the diet of barn owls and populations of mouse species across Western Europe. Pellet dissecting season runs from October until March, so this probably isn’t the last dead mouse I’ll post here.

One pellet can contain one or multiple victims, in this case three.

entry.title: Morning in Vinderhoute and Bourgoyen
entry.content:
Slow birding morning, with many birds heard but left unseen (annoying close calls: bramling, common linnet and redwing). Nice encounter with three lovely roe deer, though. Also a soaring sparrowhawk over De Afgraving (not pictured, instead, look at the cute long-tailed tit).

Two roe deer near Vinderhoutse bossen on 16 October 2026.

One long-tailed tit near De Afgraving on 16 October 2026.

entry.title: Birds wing it too
entry.content:
I aim to drop some good birds in this blog if I remember that I created it. Let the blog take flight, like this red-breasted nuthatch (picture courtesy of my wonderful wife)!

A red-breasted nuthatch in Beffe (Rendeux), LX, Belgium on 11 October 2026.
